title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
The page belongs to the setup of a vibrating elastic lamina (beam) of length AB = a. The lamina is clamped at A (x = a) and free at its end F (x = 0); y(x,t) is the transverse displacement.

On the previous page Euler used d'Alembert's principle: the inertial load p is proportional to -y_tt, and the bending moment is Kc² y_xx. Writing b⁴ = 2bkc², this gave -∬y_tt dx dx = b⁴ y_xx. Two differentiations in x then give the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation y_tt = -b⁴ y_xxxx.

This page fixes the four boundary conditions the fourfold integration must satisfy.
- At the free end x = 0, both ∫p dx (shear force) and ∬p dx dx (bending moment) must vanish. Since ∫p dx = -Kc² y_xxx and ∬p dx dx = -Kc² y_xx, this gives (I) y_xx(0,t) = 0 and (II) y_xxx(0,t) = 0.
- At the clamped end x = a, the point stays fixed and the tangent lies along the axis AB: (III) y(a,t) = 0 and (IV) y_x(a,t) = 0.
- All four conditions must hold for every t.

In §XI Euler restates the equation y_tt = -b⁴ y_xxxx. He then admits candidly that he has not been able to find its complete integral, which ought to involve four arbitrary functions. Hence, unlike the vibrating string, no solution adapted to an arbitrary initial state can yet be expected.

On the next page he partially makes up for this gap with a power series in x whose coefficients are four arbitrary functions of t, P, Q, R, S. Each later coefficient is fixed by the recursion P' = -P''/(1·2·3·4), and so on, so that the term in x^{4n} carries d^{2n}P/dt^{2n} divided by 1·2·…·4n. This is a formal Cauchy problem posed in the x-direction.
errors: No mathematical errors. The cantilever (clamped–free) boundary conditions are stated correctly, and the signs agree with the previous page.

Minor: the step from the doubly integrated equation to the fourth-order PDE drops the constants of integration. This is legitimate only because conditions I–II at x = 0 are imposed, which Euler does on this page.

ideas.what: Fourth-order transverse vibration equation y_tt = -b⁴ y_xxxx for an elastic lamina
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Daniel Bernoulli (1730s–1740s); Euler's 'Additamentum de curvis elasticis' (1744); the PDE form in Euler's later work
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I (1744); E443 (this paper); discussed by Truesdell, The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11.2)

ideas.what: Free-end conditions (zero moment, zero shear) and clamped-end conditions (zero displacement, zero slope)
ideas.modern_name: Cantilever boundary conditions for the beam
ideas.where_published: Euler 1744 Additamentum; Euler–D. Bernoulli correspondence; E443

ideas.what: Admission that no general (closed-form, d'Alembert-type) integral of the beam equation with four arbitrary functions is known
ideas.modern_name: Lack of a d'Alembert-type general solution; later supplied by integral (Fresnel-kernel) representations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Poisson and Fourier (c. 1818) for integral solutions of the vibrating-rod equation
ideas.where_published: E443 itself; the history is in Truesdell 1960

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a standard and well-documented statement of the cantilever boundary conditions. Euler's open admission that no general integral exists is known from Truesdell's history and was later resolved by Poisson and Fourier. The next page's series in x with four arbitrary functions of t is a formal non-characteristic Cauchy expansion. It is mildly interesting as a precursor of Cauchy–Kovalevskaya-type solutions; its convergence holds, for example, for time data with suitably bounded growth of derivatives. However, this belongs to the next page and is not unknown.
